found.quote: Permission to make use of AI within assessments varies depending on the module and assessment, and will be set and communicated to students in accordance with the Policy on Generative AI in Learning, Teaching and Assessment
Output, in whole or in part, of Artificial Intelligence (AI), including LLMs, where this is not permitted.
Plagiarism is the act of taking ideas or work from other sources and representing them as if it is the student’s own ideas or work.

Falsification as a misconduct type is agnostic about motivation and means: it can occur due to, inter alia a deliberate attempt to obfuscate, or inadvertent inclusion because of incorporation of outputs of Generative AI tools powered by Large Language Models.

The use of tools – be they AI-powered or not – that correct spelling, punctuation, typographical errors and minor grammatical mistakes is permitted and falls outside the scope of Good Academic Practice Policy.

The use of software or services (including, but not limited to, tools and services marketed specifically as ‘language correction tools’ or ‘grammar checkers’) to generate, develop or materially alter academic content is not permitted unless explicitly authorised in the assessment brief.
Translate text drafted in another language before being submitted as the student’s own work in the assessment’s language.
All UG and PGT students will include a declaration at the beginning of the assessment. The declaration should contain whether and how any language correction software or services has been used.
The policy here concerning language correction is not intended to impede the use of assistive technologies approved as part of a formal reasonable adjustment.
students with a registered disability specifically allowing assistive technology, are not required to declare the use of assistive technology.

the assessment instructions to students must be clear on this point; Schools with modules that fall under this exception should develop ways of consistently informing the students that this exception applies.
In determining whether an accusation of academic misconduct is upheld, absence of intention to commit misconduct, extenuating circumstances or ignorance of the rules is not a valid defence.
Students are treated as innocent until a case against them has been upheld.
Sanctions on those found to have committed academic misconduct will, as far as possible, reflect the severity of the offence that has been committed.
If the student has no prior history of misconduct, a written warning may be appropriate.
